items.title: Europe's Stoxx 600 enters correction as Middle East crisis escalates

featured_image.name: European stocks slide, gas prices soar on Iran war

items.description: European stocks plunged into correction territory on Monday as the escalating conflict between Iran and the United States sent oil prices surging and rattled investors across global markets. The pan-European Stoxx 600 fell more than 2% to a four-month low, leaving it more than 11% below its February peak, according to Reuters.[1]

items.title: EU-Mercosur trade deal to take effect May 1

featured_image.name: EU and South America’s Mercosur bloc announce ‘win-win’ free trade deal

items.description:
The European Commission announced on Monday that its free trade agreement with the South American Mercosur bloc will provisionally enter into force on May 1, a landmark step that creates one of the world's largest free trade zones linking more than 700 million people and economies accounting for 25 percent of global GDP.[1][2]

The Commission said it had formally notified Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, and Uruguay of the provisional application date, calling it "an important step in demonstrating our credibility as a major trading partner". The deal will begin eliminating tariffs on more than 90 percent of trade between the two blocs.[2][1]

items.title: Stocks surge as Trump postpones strikes on Iran

featured_image.name: Dow drops 1,000 as oil spikes on Trump's Middle Eastern regime change  adventure | Fortune

items.description:
U.S. stock markets surged on Monday after President Donald Trump announced a five-day pause on planned military strikes against Iran's energy infrastructure, citing "very good and productive conversations" between the two countries aimed at ending the nearly four-week-old conflict in the Middle East.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed more than 900 points in early trading, according to The Wall Street Journal, after futures for the S&P 500 rose roughly 2% and Nasdaq futures gained about 1.9%. The rally marked a sharp reversal from earlier in the day, when stock futures had been in negative territory ahead of Trump's announcement.[1][2]

items.title: World Water Day highlights UN warning of 'global water bankruptcy'

featured_image.name: UN Says the World Has Entered 'Global Water Bankruptcy'

items.description: World Water Day, observed on March 22, arrived this year against the backdrop of a stark warning from United Nations scientists that the planet has entered an era of "global water bankruptcy." The annual observance, themed "Water and Gender" with the slogan "Where Water Flows, Equality Grows," underscored how the deepening freshwater crisis disproportionately affects women and girls worldwide.[1][2][3]

items.title: Both pilots killed as jet hits fire truck at LaGuardia

featured_image.name: Passenger jet collides with fire truck in New York's ...

items.description:
Both pilots of an Air Canada Express regional jet were killed late Sunday night when their aircraft struck a Port Authority fire truck on a runway at New York's LaGuardia Airport, triggering a full airport shutdown that remained in effect Monday morning and upending travel across the Northeast.

The collision occurred around 11:37 p.m. ET on Runway 4 as Flight AC8646, a Bombardier CRJ-900 arriving from Montreal with 72 passengers and four crew members, was landing while the fire truck crossed the runway to respond to a separate incident aboard a United Airlines flight that had reported an unusual odor, according to Port Authority Executive Director Kathryn Garcia.[1][2]

items.title: Trump postpones strikes on Iran, citing 'productive' talks

featured_image.name: Trump issues 48-hour Hormuz Strait ultimatum, threatens Iran's ...

items.description: President Donald Trump announced Monday that the United States would delay military strikes on Iranian power plants and energy infrastructure for five days, citing what he described as productive discussions with Tehran — a sudden reversal that sent stock futures surging and oil prices tumbling hours before his own 48-hour ultimatum was set to expire.

items.title: EU broadcasters urge gatekeeper rules for smart TVs, virtual assistants

featured_image.name: Teresa Ribera - European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority

items.description: Europe's largest broadcasters are calling on the European Union to bring smart television platforms and virtual assistants operated by Google, Amazon, Apple, and Samsung under the bloc's strictest digital competition rules, warning that a handful of tech companies are gaining outsized control over how audiences discover and access content.

items.title: FTSE 100 hits 3-month low as Trump's Iran ultimatum rocks global markets

featured_image.name: Stocks: Wall Street buckles in for a long war, Hormuz is ...

items.description:
London stocks tumbled on Monday as markets reeled from President Donald Trump's weekend ultimatum threatening to "obliterate" Iran's power plants unless Tehran reopens the Strait of Hormuz within 48 hours. The FTSE 100 fell more than 1.5% in early trading to below 9,770, its lowest level in three months, extending a sell-off that has now erased roughly 10% of the index's value since it hit a record high on February 27.[1][2][3]

European stock markets entered correction territory, with the Stoxx Europe 600 falling more than 10% below its recent peak. Germany's DAX dropped 1.9%, while Asian markets saw steeper losses overnight, with Japan's Nikkei 225 down 4% and South Korea's Kospi tumbling 6.5%.[4][3]

items.title: Iran threatens Gulf strikes as Trump's Hormuz deadline expires

featured_image.name: Trump says Iran war projected to last 4 to 5 weeks, could go ‘far longer’

items.description:
Oil markets swung wildly on Monday as President Donald Trump's 48-hour ultimatum for Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz neared expiration, threatening a further escalation of the conflict that has already produced the worst global energy disruption in decades. Trump warned Saturday that the United States would "obliterate" Iranian power plants if the critical shipping channel was not reopened, prompting Tehran to threaten retaliatory strikes on energy and water infrastructure across the Persian Gulf.[1][2][3][4]

The confrontation marks the latest flashpoint in a war that began on February 28, when the U.S. and Israel launched surprise airstrikes on Iran during nuclear negotiations, killing Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and plunging the region into chaos. Iran retaliated by effectively shutting down the Strait of Hormuz — through which roughly 20% of the world's oil supply normally flows — not with a naval blockade but by launching drone strikes near the waterway that caused insurers to refuse coverage for commercial vessels.[5][6][7]

items.title: Sinopec says it won't buy Iranian crude despite U.S. sanctions waiver

featured_image.name: China's Sinopec to Slash Refinery Rates amid Crude Supply Shock

items.description:
China Petroleum & Chemical Corp., known as Sinopec, said Monday it will cut refinery runs by 5 percent this month and is pushing for access to government oil reserves, while declining to purchase Iranian crude despite a new U.S. sanctions waiver, according to Reuters.[1]

Sinopec President Zhao Dong said the company was evaluating the risks of buying Iranian oil and would "basically won't buy" it, even after U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent issued a 30-day sanctions waiver on Friday for Iranian crude already at sea. The waiver, which applies to oil loaded on vessels on or before March 20 and discharged by April 19, was intended to bring roughly 140 million barrels to global markets and ease energy prices amid the U.S.-Israeli military campaign against Iran.[2][3][1]

items.title: IEA says energy crisis now worse than 1970s oil shocks combined

featured_image.name: IEA warns world faces worst energy crisis in decades

items.description:
The standoff between the United States and Iran over the Strait of Hormuz reached a dangerous new phase this weekend after President Donald Trump issued a 48-hour ultimatum threatening to "obliterate" Iran's power plants if Tehran does not fully reopen the vital waterway. Iran's military responded by vowing to "completely close" the strait and strike American energy infrastructure across the region, raising the specter of a wider economic catastrophe as oil prices climb past levels not seen since 2022.[1][2][3]

The International Energy Agency warned on Monday that the world is now facing an energy crisis worse than the oil shocks of the 1970s combined, with global oil supplies cut by roughly 11 million barrels per day since the conflict began on February 28.[4][5]

items.title: Berkshire Hathaway to buy $1.8B stake in Japan's Tokio Marine

featured_image.name: Warren Buffett to step down as CEO of Berkshire Hathaway ...

items.description:
Tokio Marine Holdings, Japan's largest insurer, announced Monday that it will sell a 2.5 percent stake to Berkshire Hathaway for approximately $1.8 billion as part of a new strategic partnership between the two insurance giants.[1][2][3]

The deal will see Tokio Marine sell treasury shares worth 287.41 billion yen to National Indemnity, Berkshire Hathaway's core reinsurance unit, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal. The partnership will include collaboration in reinsurance and potential acquisitions, Tokio Marine said, while National Indemnity has agreed not to acquire more than 9.9 percent of the company without prior approval from Tokio Marine's board.[1]

items.title: IAEA chief says no war can end Iran's nuclear program

featured_image.name: IAEA Chief Grossi to Visit Iran May 6-8, Mehr Says

items.description:
The head of the United Nations' nuclear watchdog told CBS News that no military campaign can eliminate Iran's nuclear capabilities, warning that only a catastrophic nuclear war could fully dismantle the program — a scenario he said he hopes "will never be the case."

IAEA Director-General Rafael Grossi made the remarks in an interview with "Face the Nation" host Margaret Brennan, recorded Thursday and aired Sunday, as the U.S.-Israeli military campaign against Iran entered its fourth week. When Brennan noted that the war would not destroy Iran's nuclear ambitions, Grossi interjected: "Any war. I would say any war — unless it was nuclear war and you go for destruction in an unfathomable way, which we hope, of course, will never be the case."[1][2]

items.title: Singapore, Australia pledge to keep energy flowing amid Middle East war

featured_image.name: Australia, Singapore PMs reaffirm commitment to multilateralism

items.description: The leaders of Singapore and Australia on March 23 pledged to keep critical energy supplies flowing between the two countries as the war in the Middle East disrupts global fuel markets and raises concerns about prolonged shortages across Asia.

items.title: WMO says Earth's climate 'more out of balance' than ever

featured_image.name: Planet trapped record heat in 2025: UN | The Straits Times

items.description:
The Earth's climate is "more out of balance than at any time in observed history," the World Meteorological Organization warned on Sunday, releasing its annual State of the Global Climate report on World Meteorological Day.[1][2]

The report confirms that the period from 2015 to 2025 marks the hottest 11-year stretch on record, with 2025 ranking as the second or third hottest year ever measured — roughly 1.43 degrees Celsius above the 1850–1900 pre-industrial baseline. For the first time, the WMO included Earth's energy imbalance as a key climate indicator, measuring the gap between incoming solar energy and outgoing energy. That imbalance has reached its highest level in the 65-year record.[3][4][1]

"The State of the Global Climate is in a state of emergency. Planet Earth is being pushed beyond its limits. Every key climate indicator is flashing red," said UN Secretary-General António Guterres. "When history repeats itself eleven times, it is no longer a coincidence. It is a call to act".[4][2]

items.title: NATO chief says 22 nations joining effort to reopen Strait of Hormuz

featured_image.name: NATO Allies 'Coming Together' to Secure Strait of Hormuz, Mark Rutte Says

items.description:
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said Sunday he is "absolutely convinced" the alliance will be able to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, seeking to bridge a widening rift between President Trump and European allies over the U.S.-led military campaign against Iran.[1][2]

Appearing on CBS News's "Face the Nation," Rutte revealed that 22 countries — mostly NATO members along with partners including Australia, Japan, South Korea, New Zealand, Bahrain, and the United Arab Emirates — are now coordinating efforts to secure the strategic waterway through which roughly one-fifth of the world's oil flows. The United Kingdom is leading the multinational initiative under Prime Minister Keir Starmer, Rutte said, adding that details of the planning could not be shared publicly.[3][2]

items.title: Bessent defends Iran escalation, floats Kharg Island as 'U.S. asset'

featured_image.name: Scott Bessent says Iran understands 'brute force' as Trump weighs options  amid nuclear standoff

items.description: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday defended the ongoing U.S. and Israeli military campaign against Iran, telling NBC's "Meet the Press" that "sometimes you have to escalate to de-escalate" as the conflict enters its fourth week with no end in sight. His remarks came hours after President Donald Trump posted a 48-hour ultimatum on Truth Social demanding Iran fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz or face strikes that would "hit and obliterate" the country's power plants, "starting with the biggest one first".[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Mossad plan to spark Iran uprising stalls three weeks into war

featured_image.name: PM Netanyahu and Mossad Director David Barnea Awarded the Prime Minister's  Prize for Mossad Operations Prime Minister's Office

items.description: Before the United States and Israel launched their joint military campaign against Iran on February 28, Mossad chief David Barnea assured Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that Israeli intelligence could help ignite an internal rebellion that would topple the Iranian regime, according to reporting by The New York Times. Three weeks into the conflict, no such uprising has occurred.[1]

items.title: Saudi Aramco CEO skips CERAWeek to manage Iran crisis

featured_image.name: At CERAWeek, Saudi Aramco C.E.O. Says Energy Transition 'Visibly Failing' -  The New York Times

items.description: Saudi Aramco chief executive Amin Nasser has pulled out of the CERAWeek energy conference in Houston to remain in Saudi Arabia as the kingdom grapples with ongoing Iranian missile and drone strikes, Reuters reported on Saturday. Nasser, who has led the world's largest oil exporter for more than a decade, will not provide a recorded video message either, according to an industry source.[1][2]

items.title: Iran vows to destroy regional infrastructure if Trump strikes its power plants

featured_image.name: Iran responds to Trump power plant threat with oil warning

items.description:
President Donald Trump issued a 48-hour ultimatum to Iran late Saturday, warning the United States would "hit and obliterate" the country's power plants if Tehran does not fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a dramatic escalation in the weeks-long conflict that has choked off a critical artery for global energy supplies.

"If Iran doesn't FULLY OPEN, WITHOUT THREAT, the Strait of Hormuz, within 48 HOURS from this exact point in time, the United States of America will hit and obliterate their various POWER PLANTS, STARTING WITH THE BIGGEST ONE FIRST!" Trump wrote on Truth Social on Saturday evening. The deadline would expire Monday evening.[1][2]
